Among the discoveries were clay tablets (small objects marked with symbols), though many of the tablets were too damaged to interpret. Because Gournia lay far from major ports, supplies had to be carried inland (a logistical challenge that slowed the work). Hawes published her findings in 1908<u>—a report that included maps, photographs, and descriptions of buildings)</u>. That report (unusual for its detailed maps— helped establish Gournia as an important site for studying Minoan daily life. Although later researchers reinterpreted some artifacts, the excavation remains valuable because it documented an entire settlement rather than a single monumental building.

items.stimulus: During the 1950s, geologist Marie Tharp began plotting the shape of the ocean floor from sonar measurements. At Lamont Geological Observatory, she converted those readings into profiles (cross-sectional drawings of the ocean floor). Because the data arrived from ships around the world, Tharp had to compare measurements collected by many different crews. The first drafts<u>—although based on incomplete readings)</u> showed a continuous ridge running through the Atlantic Ocean. Her careful plotting revealed that the ridge was not an isolated feature but part of a global system. In 1957, Tharp and geologist Bruce Heezen published a map that displayed this system in striking detail. Tharp's work gained attention (even though many scientists initially doubted that sonar could reveal large-scale features—. Later maps incorporated additional soundings and made the pattern even clearer. Her maps—now recognized as foundational to oceanography)—helped scientists accept the idea that Earth's crust moves in large plates. Today, researchers still use seafloor maps to study the history and structure of the planet.
